overview.text: Natural gas is a fossil fuel found in underground rock formations, formed over geologic time from buried organic remains transformed by heat and pressure. It is a mixture, but methane (CH4) is usually its largest component; raw gas may also contain other hydrocarbons, water vapor, and nonhydrocarbon gases. In its untreated form it is colorless and odorless, so gas companies add mercaptan—a sulfur-containing odorant with a strong smell—to many supplies to help people notice leaks. People burn natural gas for electricity and building heat, and industry also uses it for heat, power, and as a feedstock for products and chemicals.

key_facts.text: Methane (CH4) is natural gas’s largest component, but the fuel also contains smaller amounts of other substances.
Heat and pressure acting on buried remains of plants and animals formed natural gas over millions to hundreds of millions of years.
Mercaptan, a sulfur-containing odorant, is added to natural gas in distribution pipelines to help people detect leaks; the gas itself is odorless.
Natural gas is used to generate electricity and heat buildings, and industry uses it for energy and as a raw material in products.
